mmp-kodaira-dimension.title: Kodaira dimension and the canonical ring

questions.q: Let $X = \mathbb{P}^n$ with canonical bundle $K_X = \mathcal{O}(-n-1)$. What is the Kodaira dimension $\kappa(\mathbb{P}^n)$?
questions.explain: $K_X^{\otimes m} = \mathcal{O}(-(n+1)m)$ has no global sections for $m \ge 1$, so the pluricanonical sequence is identically zero, and by convention $\kappa(\mathbb{P}^n) = -\infty$. This is the prototype: $\kappa = -\infty$ flags 'as far from canonically positive as possible' — the Fano case.

questions.q: For a smooth projective curve $C$ of genus $g$, the Kodaira dimension is determined by $g$. Which line is correct?
questions.explain: $\deg K_C = 2g - 2$. For $g = 0$, $\deg K_C = -2 < 0$ so all powers have no sections and $\kappa = -\infty$. For $g = 1$, $K_C \cong \mathcal{O}_C$ so $h^0(K_C^{\otimes m}) = 1$ for every $m \ge 0$ — constant growth gives $\kappa = 0$. For $g \ge 2$, $K_C$ is ample of degree $2g-2$, and Riemann–Roch gives $h^0(K_C^{\otimes m}) = (2g-2)m - g + 1$ for $m \ge 2$, linear growth so $\kappa = 1 = \dim C$.
questions.hint: When $\dim X = 1$, $\kappa(X) \in \{-\infty, 0, 1\}$ — and $\kappa = \dim X$ means $K_X$ is big.

questions.q: Why is the Kodaira dimension a birational invariant?
choices: Because it is defined locally and birational maps are local isomorphisms
Because pluricanonical sections extend across codimension-$\ge 2$ loci on smooth projective varieties, and birational maps between smooth projective varieties are isomorphisms outside such loci
Because $K_X$ itself is preserved under birational maps
Because every birational map factors through a single blow-up, and blow-ups don't change $h^0$
questions.explain: On a smooth projective $X$ a section of $K_X^{\otimes m}$ is a top-degree differential form (raised to the $m$-th tensor power) that extends across any codim-$\ge 2$ subset by Hartogs. A birational map $\varphi : X \dashrightarrow X'$ between smooth projective varieties is an isomorphism on a common open subset whose complement has codimension $\ge 2$ on each side, so pullback identifies $H^0(X, K_X^{\otimes m}) \cong H^0(X', K_{X'}^{\otimes m})$ for every $m$. The growth rate, hence $\kappa$, is a birational invariant.
questions.hint: Sections of $K_X^{\otimes m}$ are top-degree pluricanonical forms; what extends across codim-$\ge 2$ on a smooth variety?

mmp-cone-theorem.title: The cone theorem and extremal contractions

questions.q: An extremal ray $R = \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}[C]$ in $\overline{NE}(X)_{K_X < 0}$ admits a contraction $\phi_R : X \to Y$. Which property characterises a divisorial contraction?
choices: $\dim Y = \dim X$ and the exceptional locus has codimension exactly $1$
$\dim Y = \dim X$ and the exceptional locus has codimension $\ge 2$
questions.explain: The three contraction types are sorted by exceptional locus: (a) fibre-type contractions have $\dim Y < \dim X$ — the extreme example is $\mathbb{P}^1 \to \mathrm{pt}$; (b) divisorial contractions are birational with codimension-$1$ exceptional locus (e.g. blow-down of a $(-1)$-curve on a surface, or contraction of an exceptional divisor on a threefold); (c) small contractions are birational with exceptional locus of codimension $\ge 2$, the source of the flip phenomenon in dimension $\ge 3$.
questions.hint: The three types — fibre, divisorial, small — partition by dimension of fibre and codimension of exceptional locus.

questions.q: On a smooth projective surface $X$, every $K_X$-negative extremal contraction is either fibre-type or divisorial. Why does the small case not occur?
choices: Because surfaces have no rational curves
Because the exceptional locus of a birational morphism between surfaces has dimension $\ge 1$, hence codimension $\le 1$
Because flips do not exist on surfaces
Because $K_X$ is always trivial on a surface
questions.explain: If $\phi : X \to Y$ is birational between surfaces and the exceptional locus is non-empty, it has dimension $\ge 1$ (a curve), hence codimension $1$ in $X$. So small contractions — codimension $\ge 2$ exceptional locus — cannot exist on surfaces. The phenomenon (and the need for flips) only appears in dimension $\ge 3$, where a contracted curve can have codimension $2$ in a threefold.
questions.hint: What is the smallest possible dimension of the exceptional locus of a birational morphism between two smooth surfaces?

questions.q: Let $X$ be the blow-up of $\mathbb{P}^2$ at one point, with exceptional curve $E$. Compute the self-intersection $E^2$.
questions.explain: By the universal property of the blow-up, the exceptional curve $E$ is a $\mathbb{P}^1$ with self-intersection $E^2 = -1$. This is the prototypical $(-1)$-curve, and Castelnuovo's criterion says it is exactly a $\mathbb{P}^1$ with self-intersection $-1$ that can be contracted to a smooth point. The corresponding extremal ray $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}[E] \subset \overline{NE}(X)$ is $K_X$-negative ($K_X \cdot E = -1$), and contracting it recovers $\mathbb{P}^2$.
questions.hint: This is the canonical example of a $(-1)$-curve.

mmp-surfaces.title: Surface MMP: Castelnuovo and Enriques classification

questions.q: Castelnuovo's contractibility criterion states that a curve $E$ on a smooth projective surface $X$ contracts to a smooth point of a smooth surface iff:
questions.explain: Castelnuovo's criterion: a curve $E$ is contractible to a smooth point iff $E$ is a smooth rational curve ($E \cong \mathbb{P}^1$) with $E^2 = -1$. These are the so-called $(-1)$-curves. Adjunction gives $K_X \cdot E = -2 - E^2 = -1 < 0$, so the corresponding extremal ray is automatically $K_X$-negative, and contracting it produces another smooth projective surface. This is exactly the surface MMP step.
questions.hint: Adjunction on a smooth surface: $2g(E) - 2 = E^2 + K_X \cdot E$.

questions.q: Iteratively contracting $(-1)$-curves on a smooth projective surface always terminates because:
choices: There are only finitely many curves on any surface
Each contraction decreases the Picard number $\rho(X)$ by exactly $1$, and $\rho \ge 1$
The canonical class $K_X$ becomes ample after one step
questions.explain: Each blow-down of a $(-1)$-curve drops the Picard number by $1$ (it removes one independent class from $N^1(X)$). Since $\rho(X) \ge 1$ on any projective surface and $\rho$ takes values in $\mathbb{Z}_{>0}$, the descent must stop after finitely many steps. The terminal model is a 'minimal' surface — either $\mathbb{P}^2$, a Hirzebruch surface $\mathbb{F}_n$ for $n \ne 1$, or one with $K_X$ nef.
questions.hint: Picard number is a positive integer; a strictly decreasing sequence of positive integers must terminate.

questions.q: Match each minimal surface class with its Kodaira dimension.
right: Properly elliptic surfaces (elliptic fibration with non-trivial $j$-invariant)
questions.explain: Enriques' classification stratifies minimal surfaces by Kodaira dimension. $\kappa = -\infty$: rational and ruled — $K_X$ has no positive multiple with sections. $\kappa = 0$: abelian, K3, Enriques, bielliptic — some power $K_X^{\otimes m}$ is trivial, so $h^0(K_X^{\otimes m}) = 1$ is constant. $\kappa = 1$: properly elliptic — $h^0(K_X^{\otimes m})$ grows linearly because the pluricanonical map factors through an elliptic fibration. $\kappa = 2 = \dim X$: general type — $K_X$ is big, and the canonical map is birational onto its image for $m \gg 0$.
questions.hint: Match rate of growth of $h^0(K_X^{\otimes m})$ to the dimension of the pluricanonical image.

mmp-flips.title: Threefold MMP: small contractions and flips

questions.q: A small contraction $\phi : X \to Y$ in dimension $\ge 3$ is followed by a flip $\phi^+ : X^+ \to Y$. What is the defining numerical property of the flipped variety $X^+$?
choices: The strict transform of any $\phi$-contracted curve $C$ has $K_{X^+} \cdot C^+ > 0$, while $K_X \cdot C < 0$
The Picard number of $X^+$ is one less than that of $X$
questions.explain: A flip is the unique birational replacement $\phi^+ : X^+ \to Y$ of $\phi$ that exchanges the sign of $K \cdot C$ on the contracted ray: the original contracted curves had $K_X \cdot C < 0$, and on $X^+$ the strict transforms satisfy $K_{X^+} \cdot C^+ > 0$. The Picard number is preserved (since both $X \to Y$ and $X^+ \to Y$ have relative Picard number $1$), and $X^+$ is generally not isomorphic to $X$. Iterating flips eventually produces a model on which $K$ is nef — provided flips terminate.
questions.hint: A flip flips the sign of the canonical class on the contracted curve class.

questions.q: Whose theorem established existence and termination of flips for klt threefolds, completing the threefold MMP?
questions.explain: Mori (1988) proved both the existence and termination of three-dimensional flips, completing the threefold MMP — work for which he received the 1990 Fields Medal. Birkar–Cascini–Hacon–McKernan (2010) generalised existence of flips to arbitrary dimension for klt pairs with big boundary, and as a corollary obtained finite generation of the canonical ring; Birkar received the 2018 Fields Medal partly for follow-up work on boundedness of Fano varieties. Termination of flips in dimension $\ge 4$ remains open in general.
questions.hint: Threefold MMP: 1988, Fields Medal 1990. Higher-dimensional existence: 2010, Fields Medal 2018.

questions.q: Select all statements that are true about flips. (Multiple correct.)
choices: A flip is a small modification: both $\phi$ and $\phi^+$ have exceptional locus of codimension $\ge 2$
Termination of flips in arbitrary dimension is a theorem (BCHM, 2010)
A flip exchanges the sign of $K \cdot C$ on the contracted ray
questions.explain: True: flips are small (codim $\ge 2$ exceptional locus on both sides), preserve the Picard number (both $X \to Y$ and $X^+ \to Y$ have relative Picard number $1$), and exchange the sign of $K \cdot C$. False: $\rho$ is preserved, not decreased — that is what divisorial contractions do. Also false: BCHM proved existence of flips in arbitrary dimension under klt+big assumptions, but termination of flips in dimension $\ge 4$ is conjectural; what BCHM gives is termination only of certain MMP runs (e.g. with scaling), enough to obtain finite generation of the canonical ring.

questions.q: For a smooth variety $X$ with $\Delta = 0$, the discrepancy $a_E(X, 0)$ along any prime divisor $E$ that is exceptional over $X$ (extracted on a log resolution) satisfies:
choices: $a_E < 0$, so $(X, 0)$ is log canonical but not klt
questions.explain: On a smooth $X$ the discrepancy along any exceptional divisor $E$ extracted by a sequence of blow-ups is strictly positive: blowing up a smooth point of dimension $d$ adds an exceptional $\mathbb{P}^{d-1}$ with discrepancy $d - 1 \ge 1$. So $\inf_{E \text{ exceptional}} a_E(X, 0) > 0$, meaning $(X, 0)$ is terminal. (Non-exceptional prime divisors have $a_E = 0$ for $\Delta = 0$, so the question is restricted to exceptional $E$.) Smooth varieties are the prototype of terminal singularities, just as klt is the natural setting for the modern MMP and lc is the boundary class.
questions.hint: Blowing up the origin of $\mathbb{A}^d$ produces an exceptional $\mathbb{P}^{d-1}$ — what is its discrepancy?

questions.q: Order the four singularity classes for log pairs from most restrictive (smallest class) to least restrictive (largest class).
questions.explain: The classes nest by lower bound on the infimum of discrepancies: terminal $\inf a_E > 0$, canonical $\inf a_E \ge 0$, klt $\inf a_E > -1$ (with $\Delta$-coefficients $< 1$), lc $\inf a_E \ge -1$ (coefficients $\le 1$). Smooth $\subsetneq$ terminal $\subsetneq$ canonical $\subsetneq$ klt $\subsetneq$ lc. Klt is the natural category for MMP — it allows the boundary $\Delta$ a fractional coefficient, while preserving Kawamata–Viehweg vanishing.
questions.hint: Order by the lower bound on $\inf_E a_E(X, \Delta)$: $> 0$ vs $\ge 0$ vs $> -1$ vs $\ge -1$.

questions.q: Which singularity class is the natural setting in which Kawamata–Viehweg vanishing applies and the modern MMP runs?
questions.explain: Kawamata–Viehweg vanishing for log pairs holds for klt pairs $(X, \Delta)$ — the class that allows fractional boundary coefficients $a_i < 1$ and discrepancies bounded strictly below by $-1$. Smooth and terminal are special cases of klt. The strictly larger class lc admits boundary coefficients equal to $1$ (with discrepancy exactly $-1$), and Kawamata–Viehweg fails on the strict lc–not–klt boundary; one needs Ambro's theorem and more delicate arguments. Klt is the sweet spot: large enough to be closed under MMP operations, small enough for the basic vanishing.
questions.hint: Look for the class that allows $\mathbb{Q}$-divisor coefficients but stops short of the boundary value $1$.

mmp-sarkisov.title: Mori fibre spaces and the Sarkisov program

questions.q: If a klt MMP terminates with $\kappa(X) = -\infty$, the resulting variety is a Mori fibre space $\phi : X \to S$. Which of the following holds?
choices: $\dim S < \dim X$, the relative Picard number is $1$, and $-K_{X/S}$ is relatively ample
questions.explain: By definition a Mori fibre space is a contraction $\phi : X \to S$ with $\dim S < \dim X$, relative Picard rank $\rho(X/S) = 1$, and $-K_X$ relatively ample (equivalently, $-K_{X/S}$ ample over $S$). When $\dim S = 0$ this recovers a Fano variety (the case all of $X$ is the fibre); for $\dim S > 0$ the general fibre is a Fano variety, and $X$ is a Fano fibration over $S$. This is the natural endpoint of the MMP for $\kappa = -\infty$.
questions.hint: The output is a Fano fibration; what does that mean for $K_X$ relative to $S$?

questions.q: What does the Sarkisov program (Corti et al.) achieve?
choices: It computes the Kodaira dimension algorithmically
It factorises any birational map between two Mori fibre spaces into a sequence of elementary 'Sarkisov links' of four standard types
It proves termination of flips in arbitrary dimension
It classifies all Fano varieties up to isomorphism
questions.explain: The Sarkisov program decomposes a birational map $f : X/S \dashrightarrow X'/S'$ between Mori fibre spaces into a finite chain of 'Sarkisov links' — elementary birational modifications of four standard types (Type I, II, III, IV), each obtained by running a relative MMP. Together with the cone-and-contraction theorem at the level of Mori fibre spaces, this gives a higher-dimensional analogue of Castelnuovo's surface theorem. It refines, not replaces, the basic MMP and is the main tool for studying birational rigidity questions like 'is $\mathbb{P}^3$ the only smooth Fano threefold birational to itself only via automorphisms?'
questions.hint: It is a structure theorem for $\mathrm{Bir}$ between MFS, not a classification.

questions.q: Iskovskikh–Manin (1971) proved a smooth quartic threefold $X_4 \subset \mathbb{P}^4$ is birationally rigid: every birational self-map is biregular, so $\mathrm{Bir}(X_4) = \mathrm{Aut}(X_4)$. In Sarkisov-program language, this says:
choices: Every Sarkisov link starting from $X_4$ returns to $X_4$ itself, so $X_4$ is the unique Mori fibre space in its birational class
questions.explain: Birational rigidity in the Sarkisov framework means: the only Mori fibre space birational to $X_4$ is $X_4 \to \mathrm{pt}$ itself, and every Sarkisov link starting from $X_4/\mathrm{pt}$ ends at $X_4/\mathrm{pt}$. Equivalently, the birational group $\mathrm{Bir}(X_4)$ acts trivially on the set of Mori models, so $\mathrm{Bir}(X_4) = \mathrm{Aut}(X_4)$. This was the first negative answer to the Lüroth problem in dimension three: a smooth quartic threefold is unirational (a degree-2 cover of $\mathbb{P}^3$ via projection from a line) but not rational. Higher Kodaira dimension is irrelevant — $X_4$ has $\kappa = -\infty$ as a Fano variety.
questions.hint: Birational rigidity = Mori fibre space is unique in its birational class.
